strengths: Identifies and clearly formalizes a novel, safety-relevant failure mode ('3D Mirage') in monocular depth foundation models—hallucination of non-planar 3D structure from geometrically flat but visually ambiguous regions—and convincingly demonstrates its prevalence across a wide range of architectures (transformer, diffusion, commercial) via Fig. 2 and Table 1.

Introduces 3D-Mirage, a new benchmark of 468 real-world illusion images with precise polygonal planar-ROI annotations and controlled context-restricted crops (1,872 total samples), filling a genuine gap since existing MDE benchmarks (KITTI, NYUv2, ScanNet) lack 'perceptual traps' and existing adversarial sets (TartanAir-Adv, MonoTrap) are limited in scale/scope.

Proposes a principled dual-view Laplacian-based evaluation framework (DCS for spurious curvature, CCS for full-vs-crop instability) that goes beyond pixel-wise MAE/RMSE and specifically targets structural/contextual robustness, with reasonably clear mathematical formalization.

The Grounded Self-Distillation mitigation is parameter-efficient (LoRA, ~0.7% trainable parameters), and the quantitative results are strong: >93% DCS reduction and >86% CCS reduction over the DAv2-L teacher, while largely preserving NYU-v2 accuracy (89.73% vs. baseline 90.13%), demonstrating the method avoids catastrophic forgetting unlike full fine-tuning (63.01%).

Extensive and thoughtful ablation studies (loss components, training duration, per-architecture behavioral analysis in the appendix) that substantiate design choices (e.g., necessity of both L_HKR and L_NKP) and reveal nuanced failure modes across model families (structural collapse in large outdoor models, vertical-obstacle bias, etc.).
Honest discussion of limitations (protrusion illusions, long-range photorealistic scenes, single-architecture validation of mitigation) with supporting failure-case figures in the appendix.
weaknesses: The benchmark, while novel, is modest in scale (468 base images) and relies on manual polygonal ROI annotation, which introduces some subjectivity in defining 'planar' regions and may limit diversity/generalizability of conclusions drawn from it.

The practical link to safety-critical driving scenarios is somewhat overstated: many benchmark images are elaborate street-art/chalk illusions that are rare in real driving contexts; the more operationally relevant condition (restricted FOV/cropping of ordinary road textures) is a smaller and less emphasized part of the analysis.

The mitigation method (Grounded Self-Distillation) is only demonstrated on a single teacher backbone (DAv2-L); the claim of general applicability to 'depth foundation models' is not verified on diffusion-based or other architectures, which is acknowledged but still limits the strength of the contribution's generality claim.

The composite loss (Eq. 6–10) involves many hyperparameters (α1–α7, gating network temperature, ring definitions, K planes) whose sensitivity is not analyzed, raising reproducibility concerns despite the promise to release code.

Knowledge-preservation evaluation is limited to NYU-v2 pairwise accuracy and DA-2k; broader out-of-domain generalization checks (e.g., KITTI, additional zero-shot benchmarks) would better substantiate that fine-grained background fidelity is preserved.

Because the 'ideal' planar targets used for self-distillation are derived from the same frozen teacher's own (possibly imperfect) depth estimates on cropped views, there is a risk of the student inheriting or amplifying subtle teacher biases rather than learning true geometric grounding; this potential circularity is not discussed.

No statistical significance or variance reporting (e.g., across multiple runs/seeds) is provided for the main quantitative results, and comparisons to simpler baselines for the mitigation approach (e.g., alternative PEFT methods, prompting-based or geometric-prior regularization) are absent.

strengths: Identifies and clearly illustrates an interesting and previously under-examined failure mode in monocular depth estimation (MDE) foundation models -- hallucination of non-planar 3D structure from optical-illusion textures and context-restricted crops -- supported by convincing qualitative examples across many architectures (transformer-based, diffusion-based, and commercial models).

Introduces a new benchmark (3D-Mirage) with manually annotated planar ROIs and controlled context-restricted crops, which is a reasonable and concrete way to operationalize this failure mode for systematic study.

Proposes new Laplacian-based metrics (DCS, CCS) that are motivated as better suited than pixel-wise MAE/RMSE for capturing structural hallucination and contextual instability, and the paper gives a reasonably detailed mathematical formulation.

The Grounded Self-Distillation method is parameter-efficient (LoRA, ~0.7% trainable params), and the main results/ablations (Tables 1-2, Figures 6-7) show large relative reductions in DCS/CCS while largely preserving NYUv2 accuracy, which is a non-trivial trade-off to achieve.

Extensive appendix analysis (indoor vs outdoor, relative vs metric models, model-capacity effects, training-duration ablation, qualitative failure cases) shows an unusually thorough empirical investigation and honest discussion of remaining limitations and failure cases (Fig. O).
weaknesses: It is not clearly stated whether the 1,872-sample 3D-Mirage benchmark used for quantitative evaluation in Table 1/Table 2 is disjoint from the data used to train the LoRA adapters (Sec. 4.3/5.1.2 describes training with a 4:1 ratio of '3D-Mirage positive samples' to regularizer negatives, but no explicit train/val/test split of the benchmark itself is described). If the same images are used for both tuning and evaluation, the reported ~93% DCS / ~86% CCS reductions would be substantially inflated and not indicative of generalization to new illusions.

The self-distillation target for the Hallucination Knowledge Re-editing loss is derived from the model's own context-restricted-crop predictions (fit to local planes) rather than from any independent ground-truth 3D geometry (e.g., LiDAR or structured light). This risks circularity: the method is essentially teaching the model to trust its own (possibly still biased) local predictions, and the paper provides no independent metric validation that the 'corrected' depth is actually geometrically accurate versus simply flatter.

The mitigation method is validated on only one backbone family (DINOv2 encoder / DAv2-L); the paper itself acknowledges that effectiveness on diffusion-based architectures (which are shown to hallucinate just as badly in Fig. 2) remains untested, which limits the generality of the proposed 'taming' solution relative to the breadth of the diagnosed problem.

The benchmark's illusion sources (chalk/pavement art, forced-perspective murals, large-format ads) are quite different in visual statistics from the autonomous-driving motivating scenario shown in Fig. 1 (cropped road textures/phantom road markings); the paper does not demonstrate the method or benchmark transfers to genuine driving-relevant illusions (shadows, puddles, textured road markings), so the practical safety-impact claims are only partially substantiated by the presented evidence.

Generalization/knowledge-preservation checks are limited to NYUv2 ordinal accuracy and a self-defined R^2 background correlation and DA-2k score; no evaluation on standard outdoor/zero-shot benchmarks (e.g., KITTI, additional zero-shot suites) is provided to confirm that general-purpose depth estimation capability is preserved outside the indoor domain.

Several strong claims ('first end-to-end framework', 'all existing SOTA models are highly vulnerable') are somewhat overstated given the benchmark's narrow curation (predominantly artistic/illusion imagery) and the single-architecture validation of the proposed fix.

The composite loss involves seven manually set weighting coefficients (alpha_1..alpha_7) plus gating/temperature parameters; no sensitivity analysis is provided for these choices beyond an epoch-duration ablation, raising reproducibility concerns about how sensitive the reported gains are to this tuning.

strengths: Identifies and clearly motivates a novel, safety-relevant failure mode ('3D Mirage') in monocular depth foundation models — spurious non-planar hallucinations on optical-illusion textures and under restricted field-of-view — and convincingly demonstrates it is systemic across a wide range of SOTA architectures (transformer, diffusion, generative).

Introduces a new, carefully curated benchmark (3D-Mirage, 1,872 samples from 468 real images) with precise polygonal ROI annotations and controlled context-restricted crops, providing a genuinely useful diagnostic resource that current benchmarks (KITTI, NYUv2, TartanAir-Adv, MonoTrap) do not offer.

Proposes principled, perceptually-motivated metrics (DCS for hallucination magnitude, CCS for contextual instability) built on a Laplacian dual-view projection, moving beyond pixel-wise MAE/RMSE which the paper convincingly argues are blind to this failure mode.

The proposed Grounded Self-Distillation (LoRA-based) mitigation achieves large reductions in DCS/CCS (~93%/86%) relative to the frozen teacher while retaining most background/general-purpose accuracy (89.73% vs. 90.13% NYUv2, R²=93.89%), and the ablations (no-HKR, no-NKP, full finetuning) are informative and convincingly isolate the roles of the two loss terms and the risk of catastrophic forgetting.

Very extensive supplementary qualitative and quantitative analysis (appendices A–G) covering model-size/domain-specific failure regimes (over- vs. under-capacity, structural collapse, vertical-obstacle bias), training-duration trade-offs, and explicit limitation/failure cases, which substantially strengthens the empirical case and shows self-awareness of the method's boundaries.
Broad and reasonably thorough related-work coverage connecting 2D/3D hallucination, MDE benchmarks, and 3D anomaly detection literature.
weaknesses: The paper does not clearly describe a held-out train/test split for the 3D-Mirage benchmark: Section 5.1.2 states the LoRA adapters are trained with a 4:1 sampler over '3D-Mirage (positive) samples,' yet Table 1's large quantitative gains appear to be reported on the same 3D-Mirage benchmark used for training. Without an explicit disjoint evaluation split, the headline 93%/86% improvements are difficult to interpret as evidence of generalized hallucination mitigation rather than fitting to the annotated ROIs seen during training.

The mitigation strategy is validated on a single backbone/architecture (DAv2-L, ViT-based DINOv2 encoder); the paper explicitly acknowledges that transferability to diffusion-based models (Marigold, DepthFM) — which are shown in Fig. 2 to exhibit the same failure — remains unexplored, limiting the generality of the proposed fix.

DCS/CCS rely on a hand-crafted pipeline (fixed Laplacian operator, top-10%/mean-10% aggregation, multiple rings/guard bands, z-normalization) with many design choices that are not ablated or validated against an external criterion (e.g., human perceptual judgments of hallucination severity, or downstream 3D reconstruction/task error); their correspondence to real-world safety risk is asserted rather than empirically demonstrated.

No comparison against alternative baselines for mitigating this failure (e.g., simple data augmentation with texture/illusion crops, other PEFT methods, existing depth-robustness or adversarial-training techniques) beyond a full-finetuning ablation, making it hard to gauge whether the specific Grounded Self-Distillation design is necessary versus simpler alternatives achieving similar gains.

Benchmark scale and diversity are modest (468 base images, primarily street art/optical-illusion patterns), which may not fully represent the broader space of real-world planar ambiguities (e.g., texture-less surfaces, reflections, weather) that the authors themselves note as future work; some strong claims of being 'the first' framework/benchmark could be tempered given related prior efforts (MonoTrap, TartanAir-Adv) are only briefly dismissed.
Minor presentation issues (e.g., typos 'Trainbale Vocule'/'Frozen Vocule' in Figure 4) suggest the manuscript would benefit from another proofreading pass.
